extracted.intended_audience: scholars and practitioners of administrative law, political science, and interest-group lobbying; rulemaking analysts and advocacy organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and theorizing how public pressure (mass comment) campaigns operate as a lobbying tactic in administrative rulemaking and how they affect policymaking outcomes directly and indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'campaign' (mass comment campaign)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'campaign' can be defined as a batch of form-letter comments associated with an organization (Balla et al., 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the unit of analysis for mass commenting studies; distinguishes organizationally‑linked form letters from individually drafted technical comments. Practical coding guidance: attribute batches of similar form letters to sponsoring organizations and classify them (e.g., 'regulated' vs 'regulatory beneficiary').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between technical information and political information
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical information = data, analyses, legal arguments that update bureaucrats' beliefs about policy language; political information = signals from mobilization (size, distribution, intensity) about public support and coalition resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comments by whether they provide technical/legal evidence or political signals. Both matter: technical info persuades via updating beliefs about outcomes; political info persuades by changing the strategic environment and signaling intensity/representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate campaigns as part of broader lobbying strategy (mass comments as a resource)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public pressure campaigns are not an alternative to sophisticated lobbying but a resource that 'works in tandem' with technical comments and broader coalition efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing influence, consider campaigns alongside an organization's technical submissions and coalition activities rather than isolating form letters as ineffective artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalization of 'lobbying success'
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying success is 'the extent to which a coalition got the specific policy changes it sought.' (Hypothesis 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by comparing requested changes (often articulated in technical comments) to observed policy changes (e.g., textual edits, scope of regulated entities, effective dates). Requires clear mapping from stated demands to policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection effect by sponsor type (private vs public interest groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure campaigns by private interest groups are expected to be more concentrated on policies that can be influenced, creating a selection effect: private groups' campaigns should be more likely to influence policy than public interest groups' campaigns (Hypothesis 3.2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing campaign effectiveness, control for sponsor type and consider that public-interest organizations often mobilize for reasons other than direct policy influence (e.g., membership building).

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-organization leverage (use of campaigns across rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations are more likely to succeed when they lobby in a coalition that uses a public pressure campaign; use of campaigns should correlate positively with an organization's lobbying success across multiple rules (Hypothesis 3.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess leverage by comparing the same organization's outcomes across rules where coalitions did and did not use pressure campaigns, to address cross-organization comparability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct pathway: political information persuading agency officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Political information generated by mobilization (number, distribution, intensity, costly actions) may directly persuade agency officials to revise policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether campaigns produce signals agencies can interpret (e.g., geographic distribution, demonstrated intensity) and whether agency rhetoric/record indicates responsiveness to such signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect pathway: campaigns influencing elected officials and thereby agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Public pressure campaigns can affect policymaking indirectly by mobilizing elected officials (members of Congress) to contact or pressure agencies, thereby reshaping the strategic environment and providing 'political cover' or sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of congressional engagement (letters, hearings, comments) temporally linked to campaigns; evaluate whether agency decisions respond to such principal‑level signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition: agency institutional processes and normative constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of political information depends on how agency officials receive and interpret information and on legal/normative constraints (e.g., agencies must base decisions on 'facts and the law' per APA and statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional receptivity: some agencies explicitly reject reliance on public pressure; others may be more prone to political signals. Consider statutory mandates and agency culture when predicting campaign effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanding the scope of conflict as a mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns 'expand the scope of conflict', a broader category that can include giving leaders cover and reshaping the strategic environment to make policy change more politically feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a campaign broadened attention beyond typical stakeholders (e.g., attracted media/legislators/public attention) and whether that expansion correlated with policy movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement challenge: discerning influence requires counterfactual reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Discerning influence from any kind of lobbying is 'a notoriously elusive exercise' because it is difficult to know the counterfactual—what would have happened absent the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative designs, within-organization comparisons, careful identification strategies, and explicit assumptions when inferring causal influence from observational rulemaking data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political information signals: size, distribution, and costly action as indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and distribution of supporters and the costliness of actions (even low-cost acts like signing) signal intensity, resolve, and representativeness which can persuade policymakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and analyze metadata (e.g., counts, zip codes, CCs to representatives) and evidence of costly engagement to assess the informational content of campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal-agent oversight mechanisms affected by campaigns (police patrol, fire alarm, beacon, warning sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns interact with oversight: they can function as 'fire alarms' alerting principals, as beacons or warnings that encourage or discourage oversight, and thereby change agency behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating downstream effects, trace whether campaigns triggered oversight responses (congressional letters, hearings) and characterize responses as supportive or hostile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-model parameters: strategic shift (alpha_s) and direct persuasion (alpha_d)
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal models, political information operates via two shifts in policymakers' allocational bias: alpha_s (strategic shifts due to changed decision environment, e.g., congressional pressure) and alpha_d (direct persuasive shifts in normative/belief-based allocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate alpha_s and alpha_d when modeling how campaigns might change bureaucrats' objective functions; evaluate empirical proxies for these parameters (e.g., congressional engagement, statements updating normative views).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilizing the 'attentive public' beyond organizational membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective campaigns can mobilize broader audiences (the attentive public or issue publics) not just an organization's own members, thereby signaling wider public consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reach beyond membership rolls (e.g., supporters' demographics, geographic spread) and consider campaign design aimed at general public mobilization rather than only internal lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Effective comments' standard: provide reasons rather than mere reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory guidance and scholars (ACUS, Epstein et al.) suggest that 'effective comments' give reasons rather than just reactions; rulemaking is legally required to be based on fact-based, reasoned analysis rather than majority sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate comments that include reasons, evidence, or suggested edits from mere expressions of sentiment when coding influence; note that agencies and courts privilege reasoned, fact-based submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition size and multi-venue, multi-tactic mobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations with resources to lobby using multiple tactics across multiple venues over time (and larger coalitions) are more likely to influence bureaucratic policymaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate campaigns in the context of coalition breadth and cross-venue activity; account for simultaneous technical submissions, lobbying, media work, and legislative outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaigns can 'scare off' congressional opposition and create political cover
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of public engagement can 'scare off' members of Congress from supporting industry opposition and can lead to agencies receiving legislative backing (e.g., Do Not Call example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for instances where campaign visibility correlated with reduced legislative opposition or with subsequent supportive legislation, and consider temporal ordering to support causal interpretation.
